summary:
We developed Pulse-0G, a local-first astronaut health self-check and clinical escalation web application built for the Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions challenge. Instead of relying on cloud connectivity or opaque AI guesses, Pulse-0G runs completely offline on local SQLite data. Crew members tap a region on an interactive body map to view their latest reading, reference band, deviation from their pre-flight baseline, a one-line recommended action, and the exact NASA scientific evidence behind it. When a measurement drifts out of band, the app automatically assembles a structured case package for the flight surgeon.

This matters because long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars face communication delays, blackouts, and strict privacy constraints. Pulse-0G empowers astronauts to monitor physiological trends autonomously without diagnosing themselves, while ensuring every recommendation and escalatable case remains strictly grounded in verifiable NASA research.
details:
What it does and how it works Pulse-0G is an offline-first health monitoring interface designed around an interactive body map (BodyMap). An astronaut taps a body region to inspect current readings, see which reference band they fall into, compare them against their pre-flight baseline, and read a concise, one-line action backed by cited NASA evidence cards. Clinical series are stored in a local, read-only SQLite database (crewcheck.sqlite), alongside a writable annotations table for crew notes. When a metric moves out of band, Pulse-0G generates a structured Case Package ready to send to a flight surgeon. It also includes an Ask panel that optionally uses a local Ollama instance (127.0.0.1:11434) to answer questions about current status and evidence cards, falling back automatically to a deterministic SQLite-backed engine whenever Ollama is unavailable.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Zero-cloud autonomy: Works during deep-space communication blackouts or high-latency links without transmitting crew health data externally.
  • Safe, non-diagnostic boundaries: Supports crew self-awareness and timely escalation without acting as an autonomous diagnostic tool.
  • Full auditability: Automated verification scripts (npm run check and npm run check:cards) validate that every evidence card, answer, and case package traces back to documented sources.

Tools, languages, and software used

  • Languages: TypeScript, Python 3, SQL, HTML/CSS, and Shell.
  • Software & Frameworks: Next.js (App Router), React, SQLite, and optional local Ollama for on-device LLM inference.
  • Data & Validation: Custom Python pipelines (build_db.py, import_cards.py, check_answers.py, check_cards.py, check_case.py) ingesting NASA OSDR metadata (OSD-575, OSD-656, LSDS-8, LSDS-64) and NASA HRP evidence.

Creativity and key factors considered

  • Data honesty: The system explicitly separates synthetic test series from real SpaceX Inspiration4 / NASA OSDR records so simulated trends are never mistaken for flight data.
  • No-hallucination architecture: Calculations and baseline comparisons are computed deterministically in SQLite rather than by an LLM, guaranteeing reliable outputs even without AI running.
  • Human factors: Designed for fast, low-cognitive-load check-ins via a body-map interface rather than dense clinical spreadsheets.
